analysis.one_liner: Mandates stepped-up logging on national forests to fund rural counties, while weakening environmental review.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 244-173 on September 20, 2013, almost entirely along party lines, but the Senate committee it was sent to never acted and the bill died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill requires the Forest Service to set aside logging zones in every national forest and harvest at least half of each zone's sustainable timber yield each year, with the proceeds sent to rural counties for schools and roads. It makes those zones exempt from the normal environmental review process, including alternatives analysis and most court challenges, and it hands management of Oregon's O&C timber lands to a state-appointed board that must manage them for maximum revenue under Oregon's private timberland rules. It also carries a one-year extension of existing rural schools payments and some conservation additions in Oregon, including new wilderness and wild river designations.
analysis.who_benefits: Rural counties that sit next to national forest land get a dedicated funding stream for schools and roads, including a February 2015 payment matching their fiscal 2010 Secure Rural Schools amounts. The timber and wood products industry gains the most: legally required harvest volumes, a stripped-down environmental review that must be completed within 180 days without considering alternatives, sharply limited court access for challengers, and an Oregon trust managed like private timberland. Oregon mills also get a ban on exporting unprocessed logs from the new trust lands.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Timber companies and rural forest counties

how_it_helps.text: Each beneficiary county containing national forest land receives a February 2015 payment equal to its fiscal 2010 Secure Rural Schools payment, and the counties get 25% of timber revenues from the new logging zones for public schools and roads.
Rural counties that depend on federal timber payments get a permanent mechanism: Forest Reserve Revenue Areas managed to meet an annual harvest quota, so county money flows only if logging happens.
Oregon's O&C counties receive payments from a new trust required to produce annual maximum sustained revenues in perpetuity from timber.

The bill adds conservation in Oregon: the Devil's Staircase Wilderness, an expansion of the Wild Rogue Wilderness, several wild and scenic river designations, and trust conveyances of about 17,519 acres to the Cow Creek Band of Umpqua Tribe and about 14,804 acres to the Confederated Tribes of Coos, Lower Umpqua, and Siuslaw Indians.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary Americans who use national forests for recreation, hunting, fishing, and clean water bear the cost: logging projects in the new zones face a one-sided review with no alternatives considered, categorical exclusions skip review for projects up to 10,000 acres, citizens who challenge a project must post a bond covering the government's legal costs, and 2013 fire salvage projects are immune from any court injunction. The public also forgoes any broad evaluation of whether mandated harvest levels serve forest health, since the bill declares its own process the sole compliance with the National Environmental Policy Act.
analysis.who_pays_short: National forest users and conservation interests

drawbacks.text: The bill requires logging at least 50% of the sustained yield in every designated Forest Reserve Revenue Area, and states that this process is the sole means by which the Secretary complies with the National Environmental Policy Act, with no requirement to study any alternative and an environmental assessment capped at 100 pages and 180 days.

Projects covering 10,000 acres or less, post-catastrophe salvage, and hazardous-fuel clearing near infrastructure are categorically excluded from environmental review, and 2013 wildfire salvage projects are exempt from judicial review and any court injunction.

A citizen challenging a covered logging project must post a bond covering the government's estimated defense costs, with the case dismissed if they do not within 90 days, which raises the price of holding the agency accountable in court.

The O&C Trust board would include two seats reserved for commercial timber industry representatives and manage the land in the same manner as Oregon private timberlands for maximum revenue, with actions on the land deemed to involve no federal agency action.

Governors could designate federal high-risk areas for 20-year terms and have projects implemented under the same reduced environmental process, shifting federal land management decisions to state executives.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Rural counties near national forests genuinely needed money as Secure Rural Schools payments lapsed, and the bill's one-year payment extension addresses that. But the funding mechanism requires a legal minimum of logging across every national forest unit and strips the environmental review and court access that normally constrain federal timber sales, so counties get revenue only in exchange for a wholesale loosening of forest protections. The Oregon conservation and tribal land provisions are real, but they are attached to a title that transfers the bulk of O&C lands to a revenue-maximizing board dominated in part by timber interests. A bill funding rural schools without mandating harvest levels or curtailing judicial review would have delivered the counties' benefit at far lower public cost.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on September 20, 2013, but the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which received it three days later, never took it up, and it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Rep. Doc Hastings on April 12, 2013, with 22 Republican cosponsors.
The House Natural Resources Committee reported it amended on September 17, 2013, and the Rules Committee packaged it for floor consideration with two other land bills.

A motion by Rep. Ron Barber to recommit the bill with instructions to add funding for advanced firefighting and safety equipment failed 190-228, with all 190 votes in favor cast by Democrats and all 228 against by Republicans.
The House passed the bill 244-173 on September 20, 2013: 227 of 232 Republicans voted yes, 1 voted no, and 17 of 200 Democrats voted yes while 172 voted no.
The Senate received the bill on September 23, 2013 and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, where no further action was recorded before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill stalled, national forests kept their existing environmental review and public court-access rules, and the timber industry did not get the mandated harvest volumes or the O&C trust. Rural counties, however, also did not get the payments the bill promised, leaving them to rely on whatever extensions of Secure Rural Schools funding Congress provided separately.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: National forest users and conservation groups

for.name: Rep. Doc Hastings
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and managed its floor consideration, including moving that the Committee of the Whole rise.

for.name: The timber industry
for.role: O&C land timber buyers and wood products companies
for.what_they_did: Backed the O&C trust concept and mandated harvest levels that would increase logging on federal lands in Oregon.

against.name: 172 of 200 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, 172-17, and all 190 supported the motion to recommit the bill for firefighting equipment funding.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on September 23, 2013 and took no recorded action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Rep. Ron Barber
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to add funding for advanced firefighting and safety equipment; the motion failed 190-228.

against.name: The Obama administration
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill's logging mandates and environmental-review rollbacks, with the President's senior advisors reportedly recommending a veto if it reached his desk.

sides.party_line_note: On final passage 227 of 232 Republicans voted yes versus 17 of 200 Democrats, and on the motion to recommit every yes vote was a Democrat and every no vote a Republican.

industries.note: The bill makes commercial timber harvest the mandatory engine of county funding: agencies must meet annual volume quotas of at least half of sustained yield, the O&C trust must produce maximum sustained timber revenues in perpetuity, and environmental review and court challenges are sharply narrowed. County payments only flow if the industry's product is sold.

industries.industry: Rural county governments with federal forest land
industries.note: Counties receive 25% timber payments for schools and roads plus a February 2015 payment matching fiscal 2010 Secure Rural Schools levels, restoring funding many had lost. The funding is contingent on hitting the mandated logging volumes.

Logging projects in the new zones escape alternatives analysis, face categorical exclusions up to 10,000 acres, and challengers must post a bond for the government's costs, so hunters, anglers, and conservation groups lose much of their ability to shape or stop federal timber sales. The Oregon wilderness and wild river additions partly offset this in that state.
Hazardous fuel reduction and forest health projects may include domestic livestock grazing, with utilization standards not applying when grazing is used in such projects.
